cim: SJSU Conference Examines Whether Artificial Intelligence Is Moving Too Fast
cim_eredeti: SJSU Conference Examines Whether Artificial Intelligence Is Moving Too Fast
szoveg_eredeti:
“Move fast and break things” is giving way to a new mantra in Silicon Valley: Move thoughtfully and build responsibly. That shift was on display Oct. 23 at the third annual San José State University Responsible Innovation in AI Conference, which brought together leaders from academia, business, ethics and the startup community to examine the future of artificial intelligence.

Hosted by the Lucas College and Graduate School of Business in partnership with SpartUp, the conference explored the theme “Are We Moving Too Fast?” Speakers discussed the opportunities and risks of AI development, the importance of responsible governance and the challenges facing businesses, universities and society as the technology continues to evolve.

“This was the third Responsible Innovation AI conference. And the title of the conference was ‘Are We Moving Too Fast?’” said Dr. Rangapriya (Priya) Kannan, dean of the Lucas College and Graduate School of Business at SJSU. “This year’s theme was picked based on current news headlines. Media support enabled us to have a robust conversation in a timely manner. We are deeply grateful for the partnership in helping us lead the conversation in this space.”

Kannan said the debate over the pace of AI development ultimately comes down to governance and leadership rather than technology alone.

“We have people who say that we are moving too fast. There are also people who say we are not moving fast enough. But the ultimate thing is, how do we make those decisions? It’s about governance,” Kannan said.

She emphasized that business leaders must take responsibility for establishing the structures and safeguards necessary to ensure AI benefits society.

“The reason we held the conference in the business school is that this is a leadership question,” Kannan said. “Engineers can decide how to build something, but it’s the business leaders who decide: How do we do it responsibly and have all the structures in place for AI to move in a way that benefits everybody rather than harms mankind?”

Kannan also acknowledged the enormous financial investments flowing into AI development, noting that the pace of change has raised concerns even among industry leaders.

“Yes, lots of investment is going into it, and even the leaders are scared about the pace at which this is moving,” she said. “Some say this is the first time technology is moving at this pace. I don’t know that we are prepared as leaders to understand, and that’s what we are focusing on at the business college.”

While industry investment increasingly centers on AI, Kannan said universities face a different but equally important challenge: preparing students with skills that technology cannot easily replace.

“I think investments in industry are going toward AI,” she said. “In educational institutions, the discussion is how do you make our students more prepared with critical thinking skills, communication skills, interpersonal skills. We are doing a lot of that, but it’s not enough for the pace at which it’s moving.”

Dr. Anuradha Basu, director of the Silicon Valley Center for Entrepreneurship and a professor of entrepreneurship at SJSU, discussed the growing interest in AI startups among university students and how entrepreneurship education is adapting.

“In the last couple of years, students are coming up with ideas for AI startups,” Basu said. She noted that the university has incorporated AI into various aspects of its academic environment while continuing to expand opportunities for students to explore entrepreneurship.

Through courses designed to teach students how to develop businesses, Basu encourages them to move beyond theoretical ideas and engage with potential customers.

In her semester-long Venture Lab course, students develop business concepts, interview customers and create prototypes.

“In the age of AI, it’s not enough to just make a plan or come up with slides,” Basu said. “All that has become easy, but you have to speak with customers. We focus on training them on exactly what to say when speaking with customers.”

Her approach reflects a broader concern raised throughout the conference: As AI makes certain business tasks easier, human judgment, communication and an understanding of customer needs remain essential.

Vasudev (Vas) Bhandarkar, CEO of ScoreData Corp., discussed the distinction between responsible AI and responsible innovation. His company develops platforms that help organizations monitor, measure and manage AI-related business activities.

“Responsible innovation is about making sure that the innovations that are being created in the market are being deployed responsibly,” Bhandarkar said. “Innovation has to be responsible in the way it is created, taking into account for whom it’s created, and why. That’s responsible innovation, which is probably a superset of responsible AI.”

Addressing concerns about AI replacing human workers, Bhandarkar referenced discussions at the conference about the changing nature of employment.

“One of the speakers mentioned that it’s not that jobs are being taken away. Old types of jobs are being lost, and new types of jobs are being created,” he said. “That’s the important part about it.”

Bhandarkar said ScoreData develops software for venture capitalists, entrepreneurs and large corporations to support investment decisions and help businesses monitor the use of AI technologies.

“We build software to help venture capitalists, entrepreneurs, and large corporations invest better and make better investment decisions for VCs,” he said. “And then, the companies that they invest in, we help them monitor their token consumption and track it to outcomes.”

He also addressed whether government regulation is keeping pace with AI innovation, arguing that regulation should follow technological development while providing necessary safeguards.

“The regulation is way behind innovation, which is how it should be,” Bhandarkar said. “Regulation cannot be ahead of innovation because that means that people are not innovating fast enough.”

However, he stressed that governance remains essential to prevent potential harm and the concentration of power.

“There’s a great need for regulation and governance so that the innovators don’t cause harm and don’t accumulate power,” he said.

Despite the risks, Bhandarkar highlighted AI’s potential to address major global challenges, particularly in medicine, health care and climate change.

“AI can be a great boon for creating new medicines, for improving people’s healthcare, for finding new sources of energy, and to help mitigate climate change,” he said.

His greatest concern, however, centered on the possibility that people could become overly dependent on AI and gradually surrender their ability to think independently.

“My biggest concern is that people will use AI and not realize that they are becoming slaves to AI. Cognitive surrender is my concern,” Bhandarkar said. “We want people to be aware and use AI with their eyes wide open. So, we need to make changes in education and professorship.”

Bhandarkar also raised concerns about the digital divide and the unequal distribution of resources needed to benefit from AI. He said discussions at the conference highlighted how limited access to electricity and digital infrastructure could leave developing nations further behind.

“What the experts talked about was very important, which is digital poverty,” he said. “That concept of digital poverty is very real.”

He warned that the Global South could face significant disadvantages if countries lack the infrastructure and resources necessary to access AI technologies.

Michael (Mike) Todasco, a visiting fellow at the James Silberrad Brown Center for Artificial Intelligence at San Diego State University and former head of innovation at PayPal, delivered a keynote presentation based on his thesis at SJSU.
